summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

primary_citations.citation_text: North Carolina - N.C. Gen. Stat. § 7B-301 (Duty to report abuse, neglect, dependency)

regulations_applicable.title: Title 28 - JUVENILE JUSTICE AND DELINQUENCY PREVENTION (TRANSFERRED TO TITLE 14B)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Weller v. Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held that a father stated a procedural due process claim under § 1983 where he alleged that social services transferred custody of his child without any hearing, because a parent is entitled to a state-initiated hearing before deprivation of custody or, in an emergency, promptly afterward.
key_cases.relevance: It is the circuit precedent under which a North Carolina parent removed without any hearing states a § 1983 procedural due process claim.
key_cases.quote: there is no constitutional requirement of a pre-deprivation hearing under emergency circumstances

key_cases.case_name: Jordan ex rel. Jordan v. Jackson
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit upheld an emergency removal statute facially and as applied, holding that a 65-hour delay over a weekend before judicial review did not violate due process where removal was permitted only on imminent danger of death or severe or irremediable injury and judicial review was required within 72 hours.
key_cases.relevance: It marks the boundary between a lawful exigent removal and one actionable under § 1983 for want of exigency or prompt review.
key_cases.quote: Due process, however, does not always require prior process.

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals upheld the ex parte order directing the mother to cease interfering with the DSS investigation but held that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to award sole temporary custody to the father because no nonsecure custody request had been made and no abuse, neglect, or dependency petition had been filed.
key_cases.relevance: A custody order entered without a petition is void for want of jurisdiction.
key_cases.quote: a request for nonsecure custody must be made and a petition must be filed before the court may issue an order for nonsecure custody

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a natural parent's paramount constitutional right to custody may be displaced in favor of a third party only on clear and convincing evidence of unfitness, neglect, or conduct inconsistent with the parent's protected status, and never merely because a different placement would be better for the child.
key_cases.relevance: Removals not supported by clear and convincing evidence of unfitness or conduct inconsistent with parental status violate due process.
key_cases.quote: The Due Process Clause ensures that the government cannot unconstitutionally infringe upon a parent's paramount right to custody solely to obtain a better result for the child.

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed an award of custody to a grandmother, holding that a trial court may apply the best-interest-of-the-child test against a natural parent only after the movant first establishes by clear and convincing evidence that the parent's cumulative conduct was inconsistent with his constitutionally protected status.
key_cases.relevance: A removal or custody change resting on less than clear and convincing evidence of unfitness or conduct inconsistent with protected status is constitutionally defective under this rule.
key_cases.quote: the trial court's determination that a parent's conduct is inconsistent with his or her constitutionally protected status must be supported by clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for two social workers on a mother's § 1983 familial-integrity claim arising from the overnight removal of her children in another state, holding that the contours of the familial-integrity right were not clearly established in these circumstances and that the record showed neither the alleged misrepresentations nor an intrusion severe enough to violate the Constitution, so qualified immunity applied.
key_cases.relevance: It is the modern circuit authority a North Carolina plaintiff must overcome on qualified immunity when alleging that caseworkers procured an unlawful removal.
key_cases.quote: A state has a legitimate interest in protecting children from neglect and abuse and in investigating situations that may give rise to such neglect and abuse.
